title: A Semantic Data Model for the Development of Secure and Valuable Software
abstract: IT security is a crucial non functional software requirement. Nevertheless, there are several other aspects that a softwares' market success depends on. Therefore, it is vital that during the development process software developers consider different disciplines needs that essentially add value when going to market. An example of an important discipline to consider is the usability of the software, which is necessary for user acceptance. During the software development process, software developers often focus on the security aspects, while forgetting to consider the other dimensions of software development (e.g. usability or socio economical aspects). The project CUES addresses these issues by developing an interdisciplinary and integrated guidance tool, called the Wizard. The Wizard is designed to support software developers with interdisciplinary knowledge and tools during the software development processes. The core of the Wizard builds a knowledge base, which is based on a semantic data model. While the semantic data model is finished, the Wizard is still undergoing development in the CUES project and is not yet complete. This paper presents the semantic data model as a first project result and as the core element of the Wizard.

title: URGHC A Formalisation of Dynamic RDF Based on Abstract State Machines
abstract: Applications on the Web of Things require not only means to access data, but also means to manipulate data to effect change. While current Semantic Web languages and technologies are well suited for accessing and integrating static data, the current proposals around handling dynamic aspects do not provide the level of rigour required to formally specify, execute and analyse the specifications. We identify Abstract State Machines (ASMs) as promising formalism to describe system state expressed in RDF evolving over time. To be able to extend the RDF model theory with dynamic aspects, we introduce a simple rule language that is able to express additions and deletion of triples in RDF graphs. The rule language in combination with RDF model theory provides the basis for our description of the connection between RDF model theory and ASMs. The present paper can provide the formal foundation for the description of the behaviour of components as well as the execution and verification of specifications of behaviour across components.

title: Using a Block Metaphor for Creating and Representing R2RML Mappings
abstract: R2RML is the W3C standard mapping language used to define customized mappings from relational databases into RDF. One issue that hampers its adoption is the manual effort needed in the creation of such mappings. To tackle this problem, many tools with different approaches have been developed. Examples of these are step by step wizard applications, where the workflow leaves little flexibility in the creation of mappings; and visual representations, that do not support R2RML fully in a natural way. In this paper, we present a tool that uses a visual representation based on the block metaphor for R2RML mappings that is fully compliant with the R2RML specification. Furthermore, we have conducted a comprehensive user study to validate the proposed visual representation. Preliminary findings indicate that participants were able to cre ate accurate mappings; that the tool has good usability; and that the partici pants background knowledge seems to influence their perception of the mental workload involved.

title: Towards an Integrated Approach for Ontology Learning Evaluation
abstract: Ontology Learning algorithms are used to automatically generate ontologies, usually from unstructured resources. They are specially useful in domains where no de facto ontologies are available. Recent advances on information extraction techniques and text understanding such as Word2Vec are providing new opportunities for redesigning the way we automatically discover the knowledge expressed inside large collections of documents. However there are no standardised metrics to determine how good those approaches are when generating domain ontologies. Implementations need to work over very heterogeneous and continuously evolving data sources, what makes it difficult to create a gold standard corpus that allows to quantitatively evaluate their adequacy. In this paper we present a unified approach for evaluating ontology learning algorithms, which takes into consideration different lexical and taxonomic aspects that are compared against a semi automatically generated Gold Standard, minimising human intervention and promoting more replicable experimental setups. Through an experiment over a corpora of scientific articles from the Semantic Web domain, we have proven how the proposed evaluation workflow and tools can successfully adapt to different scenario requirements.

title: Actively Learning to Rank Semantic Associations for Personalized Contextual Exploration of Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KG) provide useful abstractions to represent large amount of relations that occur between entities of different types. Chains of such relations represented by semantic associations reveal connections between entities that may be interesting, and possibly unknown, to a user, thus resulting valuable for her to get insights into a given topic. For example, in contextual exploration of KGs, we may want to let a user explore a set of semantic associations that are deemed to be more interesting for her while she is reading an input text. Using well known techniques to bridge the gap between the input text and the KG a associations can be found and presented to the user. However, because of the large number of diverse associations that can be found, a critical challenge is to effectively rank the associations so as to present the ones that are estimated to be most interesting. In addition, since users may have different interests, this ranking function should be adapted to match users' preferences to personalize the exploration of KG information. In this paper We describe an active learning to rank model to let a user rate a small sample of associations, which is used to learn a ranking function that optimize the user preferences. To the best of our knowledge this is the first attempt to use active learning to rank techniques to explore semantic associations. Experiments conducted with several data sets show that the approach is able to improve the quality of the ranking function with a limited number of user interactions.

title: On modelling linked data information with an ensemble machine learning approach
abstract: Information from linked data sources is usually presented as a set of related instances that share certain features. These depend on the classes to which the instances belong, and can be related to both textual formats and frequent structures. The information can be projected onto a high dimensional feature space that reflects the differences between said classes. Through machine learning techniques, it is possible to create a model from a learning set with labelled instances by learning what characterises each class. These models have numerous applications, such as schema mapping or semantic typing. Current proposals focus on the text associated to instances by using text based features, but do not use features that reflect the relationships between classes of instances and literals, thus ignoring features that are suitable to properly model some classes. Furthermore, we have identified several problems that are common among current proposals, namely, not being able to deal with multi source datasets and not being able to model arbitrarily structured information. This motivated us to create an information modelling proposal that addresses the previous problems by means of an ensemble, machine learning approach with features that reflect the relationships between classes of instances and literals conjointly with text based features. Our experimental results show that, when applying our proposal to semantic typing in the linked data context, using these features improves the results of our model when compared to a model that does not use them, all while achieving high effectiveness.

title: Adapting Named Entity Classifiers to New Ontologies in a Microblogging Environment
abstract: Given the potential rise in the amount of user generated content on social network, research efforts towards Information Extraction (IE) have increased significantly, giving leeway to the emergence of numerous Named Entity Recognition (NER) systems. Based on varying application scenarios and/or requirements, different NER systems use different entity classification schemas/ontologies to classify the discovered entity mentions into entity types. Comparisons and integration among NER systems, thus, becomes complex. The situation is further worsened due to varying granularity levels of such ontologies used to train the NER systems. This problem has been approached in the state of the art by developing a deterministic manual mapping between concepts of different ontologies. However, these approaches have several limitations. In this paper, we discuss these limitations and inspired by a transfer learning paradigm we propose a novel approach named LearningToAdapt (L2A) to mitigate them. L2A learns to transfer an input probability distribution over a set of ontology types defined in a source domain, into a probability distribution over the types of a new ontology in a target domain. By using the inferred probability distribution, we are able to re classify the entity mentions using the most probable type in the target domain. Experiments conducted with benchmark data show valuable re classification performance, suggesting L2A as a promising approach for domain adaptation of NER systems.

title: Extracting Basic Graph Patterns from Triple Pattern Fragment Logs
abstract: The Triple Pattern Fragments (TPF) approach is de facto a new way to publish Linked Data at low cost and with high server availability. However, TPF data providers are not able to analyze the executed SPARQL queries because they receive only single triple patterns. In this paper, we propose to analyse logs of TPF servers to extract executed Basic Graph Patterns (BGPs). This enables TPF data providers to better know the queries they execute. Experiments show that we are able to reverse BGPs with a good recall and limited noise

title: Mining of Symmetric and Inverse Property Axioms from Linked Data
abstract: Presence of symmetric and inverse property axioms in a linked dataset enhances the value of its schema. It enables us to write efficient queries and to check for inconsistencies in the dataset. However, widely used linked datasets such as DBPedia and YAGO have a limited number of symmetric and inverse property axioms in their respective schemas. Thus, mining these property axioms is an interesting research problem. The current solution for the problem uses an association rule miner that does not take into account the open world nature of linked data and involves a time consuming step of preparing the input for the rule miner. In this paper, we propose a schema agnostic unsupervised method to mine symmetric and inverse axioms from linked datasets. We use the AMIE+ algorithm and the confidence measure based on partial completeness assumption to demonstrate that rules that support specific symmetric and inverse axioms can be generated. We also propose a scoring method to rank order these rules so that the top k rules can be utilized to generate the axioms. Using experimental evaluation, we find that the proposed method indeed generates axioms with very good accuracy.

title: Employing Semantic Features for Efficient Document Clustering in the Biomedical Domain
abstract: Nowadays, there are plenty of text documents in different domains that have unstructured or semi structured content which makes them hard to analyze automatically by using standard statistical or natural language processing (NLP) techniques. In particular, in the medical domain, this problem is even more stressed and is earning more and more attention. Medical documents may contain relevant information that can be used, among many useful applications, to build predictive systems able to classify new medical cases based on a set of training medical data used as baseline, thus supporting physicians to take more correct and reliable actions about diagnosis and cares. In this work we target this application. In particular, we show how it is possible to efficiently classify medical reports, based on the contained semantic information, extracted by using cognitive systems and frame semantics. For such a purpose we employed two emerging tools, IBM Watson and Framester, to extract semantic features from a collection of text documents, which have been mapped to an appropriate reduced dimensional space and processed for clustering. Experiments and results have proved the quality of the resulting clustering and the key role played by the extracted semantic features with the adopted tools.

title: Composite Semantic Relation Classification
abstract: Although distributional semantic models can effectively capture the semantic relatedness between two entities/terms, they are limited with respect to capturing the type of relation. Furthermore, an explicit direct relation between entities does not always exist. The ability to compute both relatedness and relation type aspires to human like performance to achieve the goal of producing meaningful representations of text. Therefore, to cope with this challenge, the goal is to learn compositional semantic relations. One of the methodologies is used is bring a systematic way to evaluate Distributional Semantic models under relation classification. The resources for evaluating them and methodology are not fully available at the moment. In this work, a very good dataset is created manually.

title: CEDAL: Time Efficient Detection of Erroneous Links in Large Scale Link Repositories
abstract: More than 500 million facts on the Linked Data Web are statements across knowledge bases. These links are of crucial importance for the Linked Data Web as they make a large number of tasks possible, including cross ontology, question answering and federated queries. However, a large number of these links are erroneous and can thus lead to these applications producing absurd results. We present a time efficient and complete approach for the detection of erroneous links for properties that are transitive. To this end, we make use of the semantics of URIs on the Data Web and combine it with an efficient graph partitioning algorithm. We then apply our algorithm to the LinkLion repository and show that we can analyze 19,200,114 links in 4.6 minutes. Our results show that at least 13% of the owl:sameAs links we considered are erroneous. In addition, our analysis of the provenance of links allows discovering agents and knowledge bases that commonly display poor linking. Our algorithm can be easily executed in parallel and on a GPU. We show that these implementations are up to two orders of magnitude faster than classical reasoners and a non parallel implementation.

title: An Ontology Pattern Language for Configuration Management Task
abstract: Although most methodologies for ontology development emphasize reuse of an existing one, it is still often too complex for people to understand the available ontologies to minimize redundancies via an ontological analysis. In this context, this paper presents an Ontology Pattern Language to facilitate the construction of a well founded ontology in the configuration management domain. As there are few studies of OPL for this domain, we present an initial version of the Configuration Management OPL (CM OPL) and how it was used to build a configuration ontology for database tuning domain.

title: Generating Type Embeddings from Entity Embeddings
abstract: We propose and evaluate an algorithm for generating type embeddings in the same semantic vector space as a given set of entity embeddings. The algorithm is theoretically grounded in a generative probabilistic framework, and is agnostic to the derivation of the underlying entity embeddings. It does not require any manual feature engineering, generalizes well to hundreds of types and achieves near linear scaling on millions of triples and instances by virtue of an incremental execution. We demonstrate the utility of the embeddings on a type recommendation task, outperforming a non parametric feature agnostic baseline while achieving 15x speedup and near constant memory usage on a full partition of DBpedia. Using state of the art visualization, we illustrate the agreement of our extensionally derived DBpedia type embeddings with the manually curated domain ontology. Finally, we use the embeddings to probabilistically cluster about 4 million DBpedia instances into 415 types in the DBpedia ontology.

title: SHARP: Summarizing and HARmonizing cross workflow Provenance
abstract: PROV has been adopted by a number of workflow systems for encoding the traces of workflow executions. Exploiting these provenance traces is hampered by two main impediments. Firstly, workflow systems extend PROV differently to cater for system specific constructs. The difference between the adopted PROV extensions yields heterogeneity in the generated provenance traces. This heterogeneity diminishes the value of such traces, e.g., when combining and querying provenance traces of different workflow systems. Secondly, the provenance recorded by workflow systems tends to be large, and as such difficult to browse and understand by a human user. In this paper, we propose SHARP, a Linked Data approach for harmonizing and summarizing cross workflow provenance. The harmonization is performed by chasing tuple generating and equality generating dependencies defined for workflow provenance. This results in a provenance graph that SHARP summarizes using domain specific templates. We experimentally evaluate the effectiveness of SHARP using a real world omic experiment involving workflow traces generated by the Taverna and Galaxy systems.

title: ModRef Project: from Creation to Exploitation of CIDOC CRM Triplestores
abstract: ModRef is a project from Labex "Les passes dans le present" which coordinates various projects on digital humanities. ModRef focuses more precisely on the semantic web and linked open data. The goal is to move data into triplestores also called data warehouses or collections of RDF files in order to improve the sharing, exchange and discovery of new knowledge. For this purpose, the CIDOC CRM norm has been chosen since it is, at present, the reference for the semantic description of museographic data. In order to realize the proof of concept of ModRef, a general architecture has been defined, a semantic modelling and data alignment of selected sub projects of ModRef have been proposed, triplestores have also been created. A web application has been implemented and deployed at the following link "http://triplestore.modyco.fr". This web application describes the ModRef project as well as it enables visualizing, querying and exploring created triplestores.

title: REPRODUCE ME: Ontology based Data Access for Reproducibility of Microscopy Experiments
abstract: It has always been the aim of every scientist to make their work reproducible so that the scientific community can verify and trust the experiment data and results. With more and more complex in vivo and in vitro studies and the growing usage of computers to support experiments and research data analysis, achieving reproducibility has become more complex over the last decades. Often, lack of proper experiment environment conservation, insufficient documentation and inconsistencies in the experimental data hamper reproducibility. Over the last few years, there has thus been considerable research on how to ensure reproducibility in such complex settings and how to take advantage of computer science to achieve this. In this work, we focus on integrative data management for reproducibility aspects related to execution environment conservation of microscopy experiments. We use semantic web technologies to describe the experiment and its execution environment. We have developed an ontology, REPRODUCE ME (Reproduce Microscopy Experiments) by extending the existing vocabulary PROV O. Scientists can make semantic queries related to reproducibility of experiments on the microscopic data. To ensure efficient execution of these queries, we rely on ontology based data access to source data stored in a relational DBMS.

title: Minte: A Semantic Integration Technique for RDF Graphs
abstract: The nature of the RDF data model allows for numerous descriptions of the same entity. For example, different RDF vocabularies may be utilized to describe pharmacogenomic data, and the same drug or gene is represented by different RDF graphs in DBpedia or DrugBank. In order to provide a unified representation of the same real world entity, RDF graphs need to be semantically integrated. Semantic integration requires the management of knowledge encoded in RDF vocabularies to determine the relatedness of different RDF representations of the same entity, e.g., axiomatic definition of vocabulary properties or resource equivalences. We devise Minte, an integration technique that relies on both knowledge stated in RDF vocabularies and semantic similarity measures to merge semantically equivalent RDF graphs, i.e., graphs corresponding to the same real world entity. Minte resorts to two physical operators to solve the problem of integrating RDF graphs. Minte physical operators implement a two fold approach where a 1 1 weighted perfect matching algorithm identifies the most similar RDF graphs, and a semantic merge algorithm allows for the union of these graphs. We empirically evaluate the performance of Minte on data from DBpedia, Wikidata, and DrugBank. The experimental results suggest that Minte is able to accurately integrate semantically equivalent RDF graphs.

title: Case Study of Ontology based Semantic Search in Santander Banking Context
abstract: The working hypothesis of this research is that Semantic search technique may help the banking sector to deal with information retrieval challenges in the huge amount of information available on the banking Web. In most cases, contact centres and branch based advisers struggle to look for specific information for the customer query. Existing approach, for instance, keyword based search techniques employed by the majority of the banking service provider, which makes little provision for the formulation of very precise queries. Our solution is inspired by the Semantic Web's ontology approach that describes how to enable the intelligent search capability for finding information from banking Web resources. The ontology provides a mean to create formal, machine processable descriptions of the knowledge in a target domain. The fundamental aim of this search technique is to offer better customer service and user experience on selling and buying banking products or services. In this paper, we present a prototype ontology based Semantic search model for retrieving precise answer of customer query. The proposed search system has been tested and evaluated using different search intent from user point of views, such as finding information for mortgage types, interest rates, contact information, etc. The test using the `Santander Mortgage Domain' (Santander is a British bank) demonstrates that ontology based semantic search system can perform accurate and precise queries than existing keyword search system. Originally, this work presented as part of the Santander `Big Ideas' competition in 2016, and awarded as the 1st prize winner of the competition.

title: R2RS: Schema based Mapping Relational Databases to Linked Datasets
abstract: [Extended Abstract] The Linked Data has emerged as a powerful enabler to extend the current Web of documents to a Web of interlinked data and, ultimately, into the Semantic Web. In the last decade, the diverse best practices of Linked Data, including DBpedia, have been published by an increasing number of researchers, governments, public organizations, and data providers, creating a global data space that interlinks billions of assertions: the Web of Linked Data. Therefore, the Linked Data has evolved from a practical research idea into a very promising technology that can realize the Web as a platform for intelligent information system with semantic search and querying capability. To accelerate the Linked Data paradigm in the Web, the publication of machine readable, open, and linked datasets should take precedence. Since the vast amount of the useful data are still stored in relational databases (RDB), one of the most efficient ways to populate Linked Data sets is to map data in relational databases into RDF of Linked Data. Due to the importance of mapping RDB to RDF (RDB2RDF), the multifold mapping approaches have been performed. The most important step towards RDB2RDF is two standard propositions by the W3C RDB2RDF Working Group: Direct Mapping and R2RML mapping language. By means of these remarkable achievements for R2RML, it has been expected that the seamless integration of RDB data with RDF datasets towards the Web of data can be easily actualized. However, in spite of earnest efforts to adopt this common mapping language, the publication of RDB data on the Web in machine readable RDF format did not yield the significant results as was predicted. This paper proposes a new and instinctive method based on schema translation for RDB2RDF. Since the conceptual schema of RDB is similar to ontological modeling of a certain domain, RDB schema mapping into RDF Schema is more effective than the conventional instance based approaches. We describe how to resolve the intrinsic differences between RDB and RDF in schema level. In addition, we also show the ways to map the operational differences, such as graph pattern matching, and JOIN operations. To extend this approach, we present a new schema level mapping method and an effective way to implement SPARQL endpoint in RDB.

title: TLPR: A Topological Learning Path Recommending Scheme for Learners in MOOCs
abstract: Learners in MOOCs usually have different learning backgrounds and different learning goals. To get the right knowledge from the massive courses, they need guidance in choosing adequate courses better fit their need, especially for learners without higher education qualifications. Although a variety of works about recommending related courses for distinct learners have been proposed, few of them considered the long term learning process, which leads to the lack of course coherence. To solve this issue, the TLPR scheme is proposed, which combines user based collaborative filtering and dynamic programming algorithm on graph to generate a personalized learning path. The TLPR scheme is composed of three major steps: firstly, modeling an object learners interests and finding the top k similar learners according to their interests; then, obtaining the directed weighted graph based on top k learners course selection information; finally, recommending learning path to the object learner. We evaluate our scheme on a real world dataset. Compared with existing method, the experimental results show the proposed TLPR can achieve a higher accuracy by about 5%, and it has better performance when the recommended length of learning path is shorter than 5, which is acceptable in most cases.

title: Discovering Hidden Interests for Multidimensional Analysis of Tweets
abstract: With the popularity of social networks, Twitter has become one of dominate providers of massive information. To explore the distribution and correlation from Twitter data helps the accurate personalized recommendation. On Line Analytical Processing, or OLAP, provides such an intuitive form that is suitable for people to explore the Twitter data. Unfortunately, the traditional OLAP approaches can only deal with structured data but not the unstructured textual data like tweets. The key of applying OLAP to Twitter data is to mine and build dimension hierarchy of tweeter interests. However, the current methods can extract tweeter interests from Twitter data on only a single level, but fail to obtain the hierarchy of tweeter interests with different granularity. For these problems, we propose a LDA based model, called MS LDA, which combines tweeters social relationship and tweets to extract and build tweeters interest dimension hierarchy. Such dimension hierarchy can be further employed to apply OLAP techniques to Twitter data. In addition, we employ Word2Vec to obtain the linguistic similarity of words in tweets to improve its effectiveness. The experiments confirm that our method can effectively extract the dimension hierarchy of tweeters interests, which can be used for OLAP. When compared with other similar methods, our method can recognize the interest dimension with the higher precision and coverage.

title: Leveraging Distributed Representations of Elements in Triples for Predicate Linking
abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) play a crucial role in many modern applications. Consequently, many open information extraction approaches propose the extraction of triples from natural language text in order to populate a KG. Nonetheless, most approaches do not consider forming links between the extracted triples and the KG triples, especially for predicates. Predicate linking is used to identify the predicate in a KG that exactly corresponds to an extracted predicate; this allows the avoidance of the heterogeneity problem when populating a KG. Although there have been a few studies that considered linking predicates, most of them have relied on statistical knowledge patterns, which are not able to generate the possible patterns when dealing with small data. In this paper, we propose a novel distributed representation of the elements in triples and show how this can be used to compute the similarity between predicates in order to find links that would not appear in statistical patterns. There are two aspects to the experimental study of distributed representations of triple elements: one is to evaluate the similarity rank of these representations and compare the results with various similarity metrics; the other is to use these representations to evaluate the links between predicates. We present experimental results that show that the distributed representation of triple elements outperforms other similarity metrics and the linking of predicates is notably improved.

title: Adopting Semantic Technologies for Effective Corporate Transparency.
abstract: A new transparency model with more and better corporate data is necessary to promote sustainable economic growth. In particular, there is a need to link factors regarding non financial performance of corporations such as social and environmental impacts, both positive and negative into decision making processes of investors and other stakeholders. To do this, we need to develop better ways to access and analyse corporate social, environmental and financial performance information, and to link together insights from these different sources. Such sources are already on the web in non structured and structured data formats, a big part of them in XBRL (Extensible Business Reporting Language). This study is about promoting solutions to drive effective transparency for a sustainable economy, given the current adoption and limitations of XBRL, and the new opportunities that Linked Data can offer. We present (1) a methodology to formalise XBRL as RDF using Linked data principles and (2) demonstrate its usefulness through a use case connecting and making the data accessible.

title: Entity Similarities in Large Scale Open Data Sources
abstract: The ever increasing size of several open knowledge sources enables new capabilities for comparing entities, but deriving knowledge from these sources and presenting it to the user in an understandable way is challenging. In this paper we use Wikidata, a Linked Open Dataset with more than 24 million data items and 2600 properties, to find similar entities to any given item. Unlike a vector representation where each statement is decoded to a vector entirely based on the property itself, our approach use the meta statement knowledge such as datatype and count to map properties to strategies enabling a smaller search by selecting the most informative strategies to start with, and to weight the features generated from these strategies per weights determined by the user. We evaluate our approach on the Semantic Artist Similarity dataset. The experiment shows meaningful retrievals and a 0.4 recall on the top 10 most similar artists when retrieving 100 entities.

title: Towards a framework for matcher composition in ontology matching
abstract: Ontology matching is the process of identifying alignment between heterogeneous ontologies. An ontology matching system is normally composed of a set of differently tuned matching algorithms, but their appropriateness and order of execution is typically determined by humans. With the COMPOSE framework we aim to define a holistic process for analysing the ontologies to be matched, select an optimal set of matching algorithms and orchestrate the algorithms in order to produce alignments automatically. The alignments identified include complex relations in addition to the traditional class and property equivalents. Our evaluation show that performing a lexical, structural and semantic analysis of the ontologies up front, and then composing the selected set of matchers according to the results of this analysis, can enhance the matching result, especially in the identification of complex ontology relations.

title: Beyond Time: Dynamic Context aware Entity Recommendation
abstract: Entities and their relatedness are useful information in various tasks such as entity disambiguation, entity recommendation or search. In many cases, entity relatedness is highly affected by dynamic contexts, which can be reflected in the outcome of different applications. However, the role of context is largely unexplored in existing entity relatedness measures. In this paper, we introduce the notion of contextual entity relatedness, and show its usefulness in the new yet important problem of context aware entity recommendation. We propose a novel method of computing the contextual relatedness with integrated time and topic models. By exploiting an entity graph and enriching it with an entity embedding method, we show that our proposed relatedness can effectively recommend entities, taking contexts into account. We conduct large scale experiments on a real world data set, and the results show considerable improvements of our solution over the states of the art.

title: Improving Precision of Link Discovery by Dealing with Homonyms
abstract: A key step in link discovery is the generation of suitable link specifications to relate instances from different datasets. Current link discovery techniques generate link specifications relying on attribute based restrictions. However, in real world datasets, different instances have similar attribute values even if they represent different real world concepts. Such instances are known as homonyms. In this paper, we introduce a technique that generates relational link specifications to deal with homonym instances. Relational link specifications combine a link specification relating two main concepts with a set metric restriction over another concepts related to the main ones. We have conducted several experiments in real world datasets as follows: DBLP, NSF, BBC, DBpedia, IMDB, Newcastle, RAE and ACM. Our results show that relational link specifications generated by our technique help improving the precision of the link discovery task in the presence of homonyms.

title: KlusTree: Clustering Answer Trees from Keyword Search on Graphs
abstract: Graph structured data on the web is now massive as well as diverse, ranging from social networks, web graphs to knowledge bases. Effectively querying this graph structured data is non trivial. We are concerned with a class of queries called relationship queries, which are usually expressed as a set of keywords (each keyword denoting a named entity). The results returned are a set of ranked trees, each of which denotes relationships among the various keywords. The result list could consist of hundreds of answers. The problem of keyword search on graphs has been explored for over a decade now, but an important aspect that is not as extensively studied is that of user experience. We propose KlusTree, which presents clustered results to the users instead of a list of all the results. In our approach, the result trees are represented using language models and are clustered using JS divergence as a distance measure. We compare KlusTree with the well known approaches based on isomorphism and tree edit distance based clustering. The user evaluations show that KlusTree outperforms the other two in providing better clustering, thereby enriching user experience, revealing interesting patterns and improving result interpretation by the user.

title: Explaining Graph Navigational Queries
abstract: Graph navigational languages allow to specify pairs of nodes in a graph subject to the existence of a path satisfying a certain regular expression. Under this evaluation semantics, connectivity information in terms of intermediate nodes/edges that contributed to the answer is lost. The goal of this paper is to introduce a language called GeL, which provides formal semantics for query evaluation able to capture connectivity information and output graphs. We show how connectivity information can be used to produce query explanations. We present efficient algorithms to produce query explanations and discuss their complexity. To allow GeL queries (and explanations) to be readily available into existing SPARQL processors, we present a translation from GeL queries into CONSTRUCT SPARQL queries that also output graphs. We outline examples of explanations obtained with a tool implementing our framework and report on an experimental evaluation that investigates the overhead of producing explanations.

title: Optimizing Federated SPARQL Queries using Unconventional Statistics
abstract: Answering queries over a federation of SPARQL endpoints requires combining data from more than one data source. Optimizing queries in such scenarios is particularly challenging not only because of (i) the large variety of possible query execution plans that correctly answer the query but also because (ii) there is only limited access to statistics about schema and instance data of remote sources. To overcome the former, most federated query engines rely on heuristics to reduce the space of possible query execution plans or on dynamic programming strategies to produce optimal plans. Nevertheless, these plans may still exhibit high numbers of intermediate results or high execution times because of heuristics and inaccurate cost estimations. In this paper, we present Odyssey, an approach that overcomes this problem by using statistics that allow for a more accurate cost estimation despite the federated setup. Our experimental results show that the proposed approach produces query execution plans that are better in terms of data transfer and execution time than state of the art optimizers; experiments conducted using FedX and FedBench queries exhibit gains of at least one order of magnitude in average.

title: Mapping enhanced SPARQL Query Execution with Dynamic Ontology Mapping Adaptation
abstract: Supporting heterogeneous ontologies is important issue on retrieving from and linking to linked data stored in various SPARQL endpoints via SPARQL queries. There are several approaches to support the coding process of a SPARQL query for users who are unfamiliar to code it. On the use of some ontology mapping support approach on SPARQL based query systems, we often assume that the users already have appropriate weighted ontology mappings for the ontologies used in the query. Although this approach could help users access various SPARQL endpoints with heterogeneous ontologies, sometimes we may have partial mappings among them rather than complete ones. This could make it difficult for the users to understand what part of mappings are missing in the used weighted ontology mappings to obtain their intended results in their queries. In this paper, we propose an on the fly ontology matching mechanism to dynamically generate supplemental weighted ontology mappings for each mapping enhanced SPARQL query.

title: Self Enforcing Access Control for Encrypted RDF
abstract: The amount of raw data exchanged via web protocols is steadily increasing. Although the Linked Data infrastructure could potentially be used to selectively share RDF data with different individuals or organisations, the primary focus remains on the unrestricted sharing of public data. In order to extend the Linked Data paradigm to cater for closed data, there is a need to augment the existing infrastructure with robust security mechanisms. At the most basic level both access control and encryption mechanisms are required. In this paper, we propose a flexible and dynamic architecture for securely storing and maintaining RDF datasets. By employing an encryption strategy based on Functional Encryption (FE), in which data access is enforced by the cryptographic approach itself, we allow for fine grained access control over encrypted RDF data while at the same time reducing the administrative overhead associated with access control management.

title: Time Travel Queries in RDF Graphs
abstract: We research the problem of querying historical RDF data. We formalize an extension of SPARQL, called SPARQL LTL, which incorporates primitives inspired by linear temporal logic that allow to gain conciseness and readability when expressing complex temporal queries. We give formal semantics for SPARQL LTL according to different strategies for storing historical data, underline their pros and cons, and devise query rewriting strategies from SPARQL LTL into standard SPARQL queries. We implemented our approach and evaluated both query running time and query succinctness on local and remote RDF graphs.

title: Paving the Way to Keyword Linking Benchmark: from the Problem Definition to the Evaluation
abstract: Many information systems use arbitrary lists of terms (keywords, tags, etc.) often without additional context making it hard to link them to data resources. Yet this challenging task is often a pre processing step among many, needed to enrich the original resource and its collection with new relations and properties, leading to more linked data and supporting new functionalities. We consider the task of keyword linking as a specific case, related but different from word sense disambiguation, named entity recognition in text and ontology and resource matching. We provide a formal definition of this new task and of the ways of evaluating it in a methodological and sound fashion. We created and provide a manually annotated evaluation dataset of keywords linked to DBpedia as a gold standard and experimented it with baseline methods and with a method that explicitly takes into account the asymmetry of the problem. The empirical evidence confirms that keyword linking is a difficult task, that cannot be easily solved by applying existing methods designed for related problems. This result opens up the challenge to find new ways of approaching keyword linking and bridging the gap between natural language and the Semantic Web.

title: Exploring Lexico Semantic Patterns for Aspect Based Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Web 2.0 has caused a boom in user generated content, which contains a lot of valuable information. Analysis of these natural language data requires advanced machine learning techniques. This research focuses on determining aspect based sentiment in consumer reviews using lexico semantic patterns. We propose a method using a Support Vector Machine with 6 different pattern classes: lexical, syntactical, semantic, sentiment, hybrid, and surface. We show that several of these patterns, including synset bigram, negator POS bigram, and POS bigram, can be used to better determine the aspect based sentiment, using two widely used real world data sets on consumer reviews. Our approach achieves 69.0% and 73.1% F1 score for the two data sets, respectively, an increase of 15.3% and 16.1% respectively compared to the considered baseline.

title: Automated interconnection of Linked Data applications and datasets
abstract: While the number of Linked Data (LD) datasets grows, the support for their consumption is still quite limited. Data publishers expect high reuse of their LD in different applications. At the same time, their users expect that the applications will be reusable for different LD datasets. However, the reality is different because existing LD often uses proprietary vocabularies and unique combinations of non proprietary ones, which can be seen in services such as LODStats and Linked Open Vocabularies. Therefore, it is still hard to develop applications able to consume LD from different datasets and reflect all their specifics. In this paper, we introduce a backend of a platform which interconnects LD datasets on one side with applications on the other, without the need to develop the applications with respect to specifics of individual LD datasets. The basic service provided by the platform backend is automatic discovery of so called application pipelines for a given set of datasets. Each application pipeline specifies a sequence of transformation steps which are necessary to transform the original data to a form required by an application registered in the platform. In addition, the platform is also able to execute a chosen pipeline and provide the result to the application in a prepared SPARQL endpoint. We provide an overview of the platform and present the backend algorithm for discovering pipelines in detail. We include experimental evaluation of the algorithm on chosen real world LD datasets.

title: Synthesizing Knowledge Graphs for Link and Type Prediction Benchmarking
abstract: Despite the growing amount of research in link and type prediction in knowledge graphs, systematic benchmark datasets are still scarce. In this paper we propose a synthesis model for the generation of benchmark datasets for link and type prediction. Synthesizing data is a way of having control over important characteristics of the data, and allowing to study the performance of methods on datasets with different characteristics. The proposed model uses characteristics of existing knowledge graphs to create synthetic graphs with the same characteristics, such as distributions of classes, relations, and instances. As a first step, we replicate already existing knowledge graphs in order to validate the synthesis model. To do so, we perform extensive experiments with different link and type prediction methods. We show that we can systematically create knowledge graph benchmarks which allow for quantitative measurements of the result quality and scalability of different type and link prediction methods.

title: Word Embeddings for Multilingual Ontology Alignment
abstract: String similarity metrics are used in the vast majority of ontology alignment and learning methods. Such metrics match whole string sequences or decompose them into their components to measure string similarity. However, methods purely relying on the surface structure of a string fail to capture its semantics. This issue has been addressed by using WordNet, which, however, is strongly limited in coverage of languages and domain specific terms. We propose an alternative method that utilizes word embeddings learned from Wikipedia texts, the Polyglot repository, to align multilingual ontology labels. We apply this method to two lightweight industry classification ontologies. The results show that this rather cost effective method of string comparison can generate a relevant number of correct alignments on a non standard data set across four languages. Nevertheless, the results show a low precision and recall compared to standard benchmarks. We discuss possible reasons and improvements for this result.

title: Entity Attribute Ranking Using Learning to Rank
abstract: Commercial search systems have recently begun using entity cards to support their ranked results lists. A recent study has shown that entity cards have a strong effect on user search behavior }. It is believed that existing systems use manually designed templates to construct their entity cards from semantic knowledge bases. In this work we propose an automated method for entity card building. We model this problem as a learning to rank approach applied to entity attributes. We introduce a new set of features that utilises semantic information about entities. The ranking model identifies and ranks the most important attributes (facts) of an entity. In order to experiment with our approach, we build a new dataset by exploiting Wikipedia infoboxes, whose ordering of attributes reflects the collaborative effort of a large community of Wikipedia users. This ordering represents the ground truth of our dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach effectively captures such human ordering behavior.

title: Patterns for Heterogeneous TBox Mappings to Bridge Different Modelling Decisions
abstract: Correspondence patterns have been proposed as templates of commonly used alignments between heterogeneous elements in ontologies, although design tools are currently not equipped with handling these definition alignments nor pattern alignments. We aim to address this by, first, formalising the notion of design pattern; secondly, defining typical modelling choice patterns and their alignments; and finally, proposing algorithms for integrating automatic pattern detection into existing ontology design tools. This gave rise to six formalised pattern alignments, two definition alignments, and two efficient local search algorithms and pattern matching algorithms to propose possible pattern alignments to the modeller.

title: Crowdsourced Affinity: A Matter of Fact or Experience
abstract: User entity affinity is an essential component of many user centric information systems such as online advertising, exploratory search, recommender system etc. The affinity is often assessed by analysing the interactions between users and entities within a data space. Among different affinity assessment techniques, content based ones hypothesize that users have higher affinity with entities similar to the ones with which they had positive interactions in the past. Knowledge graph and folksonomy are respectively the milestones of Semantic Web and Social Web. Despite their shared crowdsourcing trait (not necessarily all knowledge graphs but some major large scale ones), the encoded data are different in nature and structure. Knowledge graph encodes factual data with a formal ontology. Folksonomy encodes experience data with a loose structure. Many efforts have been made to make sense of folksonomy and to structure the community knowledge inside. Both data spaces allow to compute similarity between entities which can thereafter be used to calculate user entity affinity. In this paper, we are interested in observing their comparative performance in the affinity assessment task. To this end, we carried out a first experiment within a travel destination recommendation scenario on a gold standard dataset. Our main findings are that knowledge graph helps to assess more accurately the affinity but folksonomy helps to increase the diversity and the novelty. This interesting complementarity motivated us to develop a semantic affinity framework to harvest the benefits of both data spaces. A second experiment with real users showed the utility of the proposed framework and confirmed our findings.

title: Comprehensive TBox and ABox Algorithms for Test Driven Development of Ontologies
abstract: Ontology authoring is a complex task where modellers rely heavily on the automated reasoner for verification of changes, using effectively a time consuming test last approach. Test first with Test Driven Development aims to speed up such processes, but tools to date cover only a subset of possible OWL 2 DL axioms, are modeller oriented rather than with a logic based rigour of its algorithms, and provide limited feedback. We address these issues with a model for TDD testing and seven new, generic, TDD algorithms for and prove their correctness. These algorithms also cover OWL 2 DL class expressions on the left hand side of inclusions and ABox assertions. The model and algorithms have been implemented as a Protege plugin, TDDonto v2.

title: A hybrid approach for validating hypernymy relations relying on discursive properties of enumerative structures
abstract: Automatic relation extraction from texts plays a key role in the construction of semantic resources. This task can be divided in three main steps : identification of candidate relations, validation of candidates, and integration of them into existing or in construction resources. While automatic identification and integration steps have been the subject of a large body of literature, automatic validation has been addressed to a lesser extent, usually in the specific context of the extraction approach. Proposals in the field generally rely on external resources (such as WordNet, BabelNet, etc.) which are usually non domain specific, or gold standards which may suffer of imperfections or low domain coverage. We propose to extend these works, taking advantage from resources of different nature, a semantic network and a distributional resource, relying on discursive properties of specific textual units. We apply our approach on the evaluation of candidate hypernymy relations extracted from enumerative structures. Under different settings, the results show an accuracy between .45 and .71 and a gain of .17 in recall when combining both resources.

title: 3SN ontology: An approach based on the SSN ontology reuse to represent smart sensors
abstract: Ontologies for sensor networks have been widely studied in the literature, particularly by the W3C that proposed a reference ontology, called SSN (Semantic Sensor Network). These ontologies describe sensors and observations, and related concepts to provide interoperability, data gathering, sensor management. A new generation of sensors have emerged, named smart sensors. The smart sensors can provide multiple functionalities and are adaptable to several user needs. They are composed of several components: basic sensors, a microcontroller and a communication component. Thus, a smart sensor executes various algorithms and produces data combining and synthesizing basic sensors output dedicated to specific user needs. Moreover, these algorithms have to take into account the sensor features and the conditions of use defined by the sensor datasheets. SSN ontology does not allow the representation of smart sensors, their components, as well as the datasheets of the basic sensors. In this paper, we propose the Semantic Smart Sensor Network (3SN) ontology based on the Semantic Sensor Network (SSN) ontology. Moreover, it allows description of a sensor datasheet. In this context, the ontology serves as the backbone to a system that provides assistance upon the design and operation of Smart Sensors in sportswear. As a validation phase to the later proposed approach, we apply our ontology on two sports activity scenarios.

title: Semantic Trajectories Revisited: An Ontological Framework for Semantically Enriched Trajectories for Movement Analysis.
abstract: Analysis of moving objects behaviour requires spatio temporal data concerning objects' positional information, enriched with contextual information. Contextual information is a generic term referring to any type of information about entities affecting the behaviour of an object (e.g. weather conditions, or events of special interest), and entities that are being affected by the behaviour of an object (e.g. an airspace sector or a fishing area). Further to this, the context of an objects' trajectory may include the trajectories of other objects in its vicinity. The semantic description of moving objects trajectories and their semantic enrichment via linking them to semantically described contextual information is important to ontology supported tasks regarding Maritime Situation Awareness (MSA) and Air Traffic Management (ATM). To a greater extent than previous works, this paper proposes a generic ontology for the representation of moving objects' trajectories at different spatio temporal levels of analysis, in association with different types of contextual information. We demonstrate the benefits of the ontological constructs used for the provision of semantically annotated data concerning objects' trajectories, linked with contextual information via SPARQL queries.

title: Removing Barriers to Transparency: a Case Study on the Use of Semantic Technologies to Tackle Procurement Data Inconsistency
abstract: Public Procurement (PP) information, made available as Open Government Data (OGD), leads to tangible benefits to identify government spending for goods and services. Nevertheless, making data freely available is a necessary, but not sufficient condition for improving transparency. Fragmentation of OGD due to diverse processes adopted by different administrations and inconsistency within data affect opportunities to obtain valuable information. In this article, we propose a solution based on linked data to integrate existing datasets and to enhance information coherence. We present an application of such principles through a semantic layer built on Italian PP information available as OGD. As result, we overcame the fragmentation of datasources and increased the consistency of information, enabling new opportunities for analyzing data to fight corruption and for raising competition between companies in the market.

title: Exploring Importance Measures for Summarizing RDF/S KBs
abstract: Given the explosive growth in the size and the complexity of the Data Web, there is now more than ever, an increasing need to develop methods and tools in order to facilitate the understanding and exploration of RDF/S Knowledge Bases (KBs). To this direction, summarization approaches try to produce an abridged version of the original data source, highlighting the most representative concepts. Central questions to summarization are: how to identify the most important nodes and then how to link them in order to produce a valid sub schema graph. In this paper, we try to answer the first question by revisiting six well known measures from graph theory and adapting them for RDF/S KBs. Then, we proceed further to model the problem of linking those nodes as a graph Steiner Tree problem (GSTP) employing approximations and heuristics to speed up the execution of the respective algorithms. The performed experiments show the added value of our approach since a) our adaptations outperform current state of the art measures for selecting the most important nodes and b) the constructed summary has a better quality in terms of the additional nodes introduced to the generated summary.

title: Towards a Use Case Driven Evaluation of Database Systems for RDF Data Storage
abstract: There is a growing number of database systems available: from traditional relational databases to RDF triple stores, not to mention the area of NoSQL technologies. For an application developer it is hard to decide which system to choose for RDF data storage in order to reach optimal overall query performance. Comparisons of database systems often use benchmarks to conclude systems with best overall runtime. However, the structure of data and queries used in traditional benchmarks differ from real world environments. They are typically not aligned with their application use case. In this paper we address the issue of the choice for a database system for RDF data management with respect to optimized overall query runtime performance. We investigate a use case driven approach where queries are grouped by means of a global application use case. We evaluate heterogeneous database systems with real world application data and measure query runtime performance. The evaluation results show that the choice for a database system should not only be based on the overall query runtimes, as traditional benchmark results would suggest, but preferably according to the use cases of the application itself.

title: The role of ontology summarization in semantics aware recommender systems
abstract: In the current information centric era, recommender systems are gaining momentum as tools able to assist users in daily decision making tasks. They may exploit users' past behavior combined with side/contextual information to suggest them new items or pieces of knowledge they might be interested in. Within the recommendation process, Linked Data (LD) have been already proposed as a valuable source of information to enhance the predictive power of recommender systems not only in terms of accuracy but also of diversity and novelty of results. In this direction, one of the main open issues in using LD to feed a recommendation engine is related to feature selection: how to select only the most relevant subset of the original LD dataset thus avoiding both useless processing of data and the so called ``course of dimensionality'' problem. In this paper we show that ontology summarization may play a relevant role in selecting properties/features useful to a recommender system. In particular, we compare an approach based on ontology summarization with a classical one, i.e., Information Gain. We evaluated the performance of the two methods in terms of accuracy and aggregate diversity by setting up an experimental testbed relying on datasets related to three different knowledge domains: movies, books and music.

title: Towards Semantic Storytelling through Knowledge Rich Relation Extraction
abstract: The ever growing amount of digital information and their heterogeneous nature poses multiple challenges for information analysts. We are experimenting with an approach to overcome these challenges by supporting human experts we call them digital curators or knowledge workers in their analyses of arbitrary document collections by applying several fully automatic semantic processing techniques to these document collections in order to enable the human experts to concentrate on their core objectives and use cases such as, among others, journalism, tv programme production or exhibition design. Part of this toolbox of Digital Curation Technologies is a novel semantic processing approach that we call Semantic Storytelling. The current prototype exploits a pipeline of NLP methods to generate a semantic layer that is used at a later stage for the generation of stories. The system uses semantic story templates, which are automatically generated by a training procedure. The actual stories are generated by extracting information from the document collection and removing irrelevant information to arrive at the information required to fill the template slots. This paper explains the training procedure and the processing pipeline that is used to arrive at the required information. Alternative approaches are discussed and evaluated using a corpus of manually annotated biographies.

title: Ontological Modelling of Situational Awareness in Surgical Interventions
abstract: Optical navigation systems are the means of choice to overcome spatial association problems of the endoscopic imaging in minimally invasive surgery. Using optical markers, the patient's real position, his medical imaging data and surgical tool locations are mapped into the same workspace. Such visual based assistance systems however, suffer from their technical requirements. The BIOPASS project aims to develop a navigation system based on a novel markerless localization method that uses only the current surgical situation and the procedures history to identify the present anatomy. The ontology, presented in this paper, plays an integral part in this system as it translates the situational information of a surgical procedure into an internal machine readable representation. This combines multi modal sensor data, e.g. endoscopic images, endoscope movement or surgical work steps, to allow a classification of the apparent situation and provide navigation support based on identified anatomical landmark and work step.

title: NdFluents: An Ontology for Annotating Statements in Linked Data
abstract: RDF provide the means to publish, link, and consume heterogeneous information on the Web of Data, whereas OWL allows to build and ontology and infer new information that is implicit in the data. Annotating this data with additional information, such as provenance, trustworthiness, or temporal validity is becoming more and more important in recent times; however, RDF and OWL only allow to natively represent binary (or dyadic) relations between entities. While there are some approaches to represent metadata on RDF, they lose most of the reasoning power of OWL. In this paper we present an extension of Welty and Fikes' 4dFluents ontology on associating temporal validity to statements to any context dimension, comparing it with alternative representations, and provide guidelines and design patterns to implement it on actual data.

title: IDOL: Comprehensive & Complete LOD Insights
abstract: Over the last decade, we observed a steadily increasing amount of RDF datasets made available on the web of data. The decentralized nature of the web, however, makes it hard to identify all these datasets. Even more so, when downloadable data distributions are discovered, only insufficient metadata is available to describe the datasets properly, thus posing barriers on its usefulness and reuse. In this paper, we describe an attempt to exhaustively identify the whole linked open data cloud by harvesting metadata from multiple sources, providing insights about duplicated data and the general quality of the available metadata. This was only possible by using a probabilistic data structure called Bloom filter. Finally, we enrich existing dataset metadata with our approach and republish them through an SPARQL endpoint.

title: Traffic Analytics for Linked Data Publishers
abstract: We present a traffic analytics platform for servers that publish Linked Data. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first system that mines access logs of registered Linked Data servers to extract traffic insights on daily basis and without human intervention. The framework extracts Linked Data specific traffic metrics from log records of HTTP lookups and SPARQL queries, and provides insights not available in traditional web analytics tools. Among all, we detect visitor sessions with a variant of hierarchical agglomerative clustering. We also identify workload peaks of SPARQL endpoints by detecting heavy and light SPARQL queries with supervised learning. The platform has been tested on two years of access logs of the British National Bibliography RDF dataset.

title: Modeling and Querying Greek Legislation using Semantic Web Technologies
abstract: In this work, we study how one can make legislation available as open data using semantic web technologies. We focus on Greek legislation and show how it can be modeled using ontologies expressed in OWL and RDF, and queried using SPARQL. To demonstrate the applicability and usefulness of our approach, we develop a web application, called Nomothesia, which makes Greek legislation easily accessible to the public. Nomothesia offers advanced services for retrieving and querying Greek legislation and is intended for citizens through intuitive presentational views and search interfaces, but also for application developers that would like to consume content through two web services: a SPARQL endpoint and a RESTful API. Opening up legislation in this way is a great leap towards making governments accountable to citizens and increasing transparency.

title: Supporting Ontology Engineering with OnToology
abstract: Due to the increasing uptake of semantic technologies, ontologies have started becoming a commodity within many collaborative software development projects. As a result, several challenges arise for those teams that have to deal with the interaction between usual ontology engineering activities and software development practices. In this paper we mainly focus on challenges related to ontology development support activities (documentation, evaluation, releasing and publishing), and describe how we have addressed them by providing tool support for them. Our proposed Web based application, OnToology, builds on top of git based environments (e.g. GitHub), providing features specific for ontologies that improve and ease their development process in a collaborative manner. We have validated OnToology against a set of the most representative requirements for ontology support activities in distributed development environments, and evaluated its features and usability over several development projects, involving 54 users from different communities.

title: entity2vec: Unsupervised Feature Learning for Knowledge Graphs Embeddings
abstract: Knowledge Graphs gather an enormous amount of valuable information about real world entities, which are represented as nodes connected to other nodes by semantic properties. Feature learning algorithms aim to project entities into a low dimensional space, turning them into vectors, in a way that is preserving semantic similarities. Existing systems rely on a rigid definition of the neighborhood of an entity, which is not adaptable to the diversity of connectivity patterns that Knowledge Graphs can present. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised feature learning approach that adapts neural language modeling to Knowledge Graphs, using a general definition of neighborhood of an entity that is based on second order random walks. Our evaluation shows that this approach outperforms state of the art performance on a set of supervised learning tasks on Knowledge Graphs over a collection of well known benchmark datasets (AIFB, AM, BGS, MUTAG).

title: Harnessing Diversity in Crowds and Machines for Better NER performance
abstract: Over the last years information extraction tools have gained a great popularity and brought significant improvement in performance in extracting meaning from structured or unstructured data. For example, named entity recognition (NER) tools identify types such as people, organizations or places in text. However, despite their high F1 performance, NER tools are still prone to brittleness due to their highly specialized and constrained input and training data. Thus, each tool is able to extract only a subset of the named entities (NE) mentioned in a given text. In order to improve the NE Coverage we propose a hybrid approach, where we first aggregate the output of various NER tools and then validate and extend it through crowdsourcing. The results from our experiments show that this approach performs significantly better than the individual state of the art tools (including existing tools that integrate individual outputs already). Furthermore, we show that the crowd is quite effective in (1) identifying mistakes, inconsistencies and ambiguities in currently used gold standards, as well as in (2) a promising approach to gather ground truth annotations for NER that capture a multitude of opinions.

title: Cross Language Information Retrieval based on Bilingual Formal Concept Analysis
abstract: We propose and evaluate a Cross language Information Retrieval model that avoids query and/or document translation. The model uses Formal Concept Analysis to extract bilingual Closed Concept used as a resource to build bilingual documents and their indexes. Moreover, the results of using noun phrases in addition to keyword, to index queries and documents have been studied. We report the evaluation results on an Italian French collection and an English French collection. Our main finding suggests that Formal Concept Analysis is effective to build multilingual documents and noun phrases components should be used with keywords for multilingual documents indexing.

title: A SPARQL extension for generating RDF from heterogeneous formats
abstract: RDF aims at being the universal abstract data model for structured data on the Web. While there is effort to convert data in RDF, the vast majority of data available on the Web does not conform to RDF. Indeed, exposing data in RDF, either natively or through wrappers, can be very costly. Furthermore, in the emerging Web of Things, resource constraints of devices prevent from processing RDF graphs. Hence one cannot expect that all the data on the Web be available as RDF anytime soon. Several tools can generate RDF from non RDF data, and transformation or mapping languages have been designed to offer more flexible solutions (GRDDL, XSPARQL, R2RML, RML, CSVW, etc.). In this paper, we introduce a new language, SPARQL Generate, that generates RDF from: (i) a RDF Dataset, and (ii) a set of documents in arbitrary formats. As SPARQL Generate is designed as an extension of SPARQL 1.1, it can provably: (i) be implemented on top on any existing SPARQL engine, and (ii) leverage the SPARQL extension mechanism to deal with an open set of formats. Furthermore, we show evidence that (iii) it can be easily learned by knowledge engineers that know SPARQL 1.1, and (iv) our first naive open source implementation performs better than the reference implementation of RML for big transformations.

title: Improving Machine Translation through Linked Data
abstract: With the increasing availability of multilingual linked lexical resources on the web, there is a renewed interest in fashioning Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications such as Machine Translation (MT) to comply to the Semantic Web technology paradigm. Automatic translation systems still are not perfect. Unknown words and ambiguous translations are among the most common sources of error in MT outputs. In this paper, we attempt to minimise these errors by interfacing Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) models with Linked Open Data (LOD) resources such as DBpedia and BabelNet. We demonstrate our experiments on the open source SMT system Moses and evaluate multiple strategies for exploiting knowledge from multilingual linked data in automatically translating named entities. We conclude with an analysis of best practices for multilingual linked data sets so as to optimise their benefit to multilingual and cross lingual technology solutions.

title: Tuning Personalized PageRank for Semantics aware Recommendations based on Linked Open Data
abstract: In this article we investigate how the knowledge available in the Linked Open Data cloud (LOD) can be exploited to improve the effectiveness of a semantics aware graph based recommendation framework based on Personalized PageRank (PPR). In our approach we extended the classic {bipartite data model, in which only user item relationships are modeled, by injecting some of the exogenous knowledge about the items which is available in the LOD cloud. Our approach works in two steps: first, all the available items are automatically mapped to a DBpedia node; next, all the properties gathered from DBpedia that describe the item are connected to the item nodes, thus enriching the original representation and giving rise to a tripartite data model. Such a data model can be easily exploited to provide users with recommendations by running PPR against the resulting representation and by suggesting the items with the highest PageRank score. In the experimental evaluation carried out against two datasets, we showed that our semantics aware recommendation framework exploiting DBpedia and PPR can overcome the performance of several state of the art approaches. Moreover, a proper tuning of PPR parameters, obtained by better distributing the weights among the nodes modeled in the graph, further improved the overall accuracy of the framework and definitely confirmed the effectiveness of our strategy.

title: Improving the Classification of Events in Tweets using Semantic Enrichment
abstract: Contextual enrichment using external sources has been proposed as a means to deal with the poor textual contents of tweets for event classification. Related work performs contextual enrichment according to specific assumptions about the events. Furthermore, enrichment adds a significant amount of extra features, most of them with no discriminative contribution to the event classification task. In this paper, we propose an enrichment framework process targeted at the classification of events in general, of which the key elements are: a) external enrichment using related web pages for extending the conceptual features contained within the tweets; b) semantic enrichment using the Linked Open Data cloud to add related semantic features, and c) a pruning technique that selects the semantic features with discriminative potential. We compared the proposed approach against a word embeddings classification baseline using seven different event datasets. Our experiments reveal that the process framework supports the classification of distinct event types, outperforming the baseline in 94\% of the cases, with an average improvement of 12.2 percentage points in the F measure.

title: Combining word and entity embeddings for entity linking
abstract: The correct identification of the link between an entity mention in a text and a known entity in a large knowledge base is important in information retrieval or information extraction. The general approach for this task is to generate, for a given mention, a set of candidate entities from the base and, in a second step, determine which is the best one. This paper proposes a novel method for the second step which is based on the joint learning of embeddings for the words in the text and the entities in the knowledge base. By learning these embeddings in the same space we arrive at a more conceptually grounded model that can be used for candidate selection based on the surrounding context. The relative improvement of this approach is experimentally validated on a benchmark corpus from the TAC EDL 2015 evaluation campaign.

title: Game Character Ontology (GCO) A vocabulary for extracting and describing game character information from fansites
abstract: Creating video games that are market competent costs in time, effort and resources which often cannot be afforded by small medium enterprises, especially by independent game development studios. As most of the tasks involved in developing games are labour and creativity intensive, our vision is to reduce software development effort and enhance design creativity by automatically generating novel and semantically enriched content for games from Web sources. In particular, this paper presents a vocabulary that defines detailed properties used for describing video game characters information extracted from sources such as fansites to create game character models.
